title: Components, JSX, and Props
summary: Write components as TypeScript functions that return JSX, pass data with props and children, render conditionally and in lists, and style them.
intro: Every screen in a React app, from one product card to a whole checkout page, is built from components: small functions you write once and use wherever you need them. To build Trailhead, the outdoor gear shop this course works toward, you need to write them well. This lesson starts with JSX, the HTML-like code components return, and what it turns into. Then come props, for passing data in, and children, for wrapping one component around others. After that: showing things only sometimes, turning a list of data into a list on screen, and styling. The code here is for reading. The next lesson creates a project on your computer, where you can try every example.

steps.title: JSX is JavaScript
steps.body:
Every component you write returns JSX, and JSX looks so much like HTML that it's easy to forget it isn't. Knowing what it really is explains the rules that trip people up at first: why it's `className` and not `class`, what the curly braces do, and why a component can't return two tags side by side. ## Tags inside JavaScript **JSX** is a way to write HTML-like tags right inside JavaScript. The name comes from JavaScript and XML, an older markup language built from tags too. Here's a line of it: ```tsx export const title =

Trail gear

; ``` There are no quotes around the tag, so it isn't a string. It's a value, kept in a variable like any other. Files that hold JSX end in `.jsx`, or in `.tsx` when they also use TypeScript, which the next part introduces. No browser can read JSX. Before your code reaches the browser, a **compiler**, a program that rewrites code from one form into another, turns every tag into an ordinary function call. In a React project, Vite does this as part of the transform step you met in the web course, so you never run it yourself. Here's what it made of that line: ```javascript import { jsx as _jsx } from "react/jsx-runtime"; export const title = /* @__PURE__ */ _jsx("h1", { className: "title", children: "Trail gear" }); ``` The tag became a call to `jsx()`, a function from React that the compiler imported at the top. Its first argument is the tag's name. Its second is an object with the attributes, plus a field called `children` for whatever sat between the opening and closing tags. The comment in the middle is a note for the bundler: if nothing uses the result, it can drop the call. ## Elements are objects When that call runs, it returns an **element**: a plain JavaScript object that describes what you want on the screen. Printed with `console.log`, the element looks like this: ```text { '$$typeof': Symbol(react.transitional.element), type: 'h1', key: null, ref: null, props: { className: 'title', children: 'Trail gear' } } ``` `type` says what to make, an `h1`, and `props` holds its attributes and children. `$$typeof` marks the object as a real React element. `key` comes up in the part on lists, and `ref` in the Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs lesson. While you're developing, React adds a couple of fields of its own, for its warnings. An element isn't a DOM node, and making one puts nothing on the screen. It's a description, cheap to make and cheap to throw away. React reads a whole tree of them, compares it with the last tree, and changes only the DOM that's different: the diffing you met in the Why React Exists lesson. In the diagram, steps 1 and 2 happen on your computer, and steps 3 and 4 in the browser. ```diagram components-and-jsx-compile JSX is shorthand for a function call, and the call makes an object that React DOM turns into a node. ``` ## The rules come from JavaScript Since every tag becomes a function call, JSX follows JavaScript's rules, not HTML's: - **Curly braces hold JavaScript.** Between tags, `{product.name}` puts a value on the page, and an attribute takes one the same way, as in `src={product.imageUrl}`. Quotes are only for fixed text. A brace holds an **expression**, a piece of code that produces a value, like a variable, a sum, or a function call. `if` and `for` produce no value, so they can't go in braces, and part 4 shows what to use instead. - **Attributes use the DOM's property names.** `class` is a reserved word in JavaScript, so JSX uses `className`, the name of the same property on a DOM element. A label's `for` becomes `htmlFor` for the same reason. Names made of several words are written in **camelCase**, each word after the first starting with a capital: `onClick`, `tabIndex`, `maxLength`. Only `aria-*` and `data-*` attributes keep their dashes. - **Every tag closes.** HTML lets `` and `` stand alone. In JSX they're `` and ``, so the compiler knows where each call ends. - **One outer tag.** A function returns one value, so a piece of JSX has one outer tag. To return two tags side by side without wrapping them in a `div` you don't need, put them in a **fragment**, written `<>` and ``. It groups them and adds nothing to the page. ## Text is always text A string in braces shows up as text, exactly as it is, even when it looks like HTML. React sets text the safe way, like `textContent` in the web course and never like `innerHTML`, so the cross-site scripting attack you met there can't come in through braces. The Web Vulnerabilities and Secrets lesson covers the few ways around this, and why to avoid them.

examples.title: Braces, attributes, and a fragment
examples.prompt: A component, `src/components/ProductSummary.tsx`, that uses each rule. The output is the HTML React put on the page, copied from the Elements panel in DevTools.
examples.output:
Trail Pack 45L

$189.00, or $47.25 a month
examples.explanation: `formatPrice` comes from `src/lib/format.ts`, a small helper that turns whole cents into dollars with JavaScript's built-in `Intl.NumberFormat`, so 18900 becomes $189.00. Each pair of braces holds an expression: a variable, a function call, even a sum inside the call, `priceCents / 4`. `min={1}` passes a number, while `"number"` in quotes is fixed text. In the output, `className` became `class` and `htmlFor` became `for`, and the input closes with `/>` in the JSX but not in the HTML. The fragment left no trace: the four tags sit side by side with no wrapper. Don't worry yet about how the component itself works. That's the next part.

examples.title: Text in braces stays text
examples.prompt: A review with HTML in it, from someone trying to run a script on your page, in `src/components/ReviewText.tsx`.
examples.explanation: If this string went in through `innerHTML`, the browser would make an `img` tag, fail to load the picture at `x`, and run the `onerror` code, an attack you met in the web course. Here it doesn't. React put the string in as text, so the browser wrote `<` as `<` and `>` as `>`, the codes HTML uses to show those characters instead of starting a tag. On the screen, the paragraph shows the whole string, angle brackets and all, then Great pack!. You get this for free on every string you put in braces, which is a big reason React pages are safer by default than hand-written DOM code.

steps.title: Components and props

examples.title: Two cards from one component
examples.prompt: `src/App.tsx` shows two products with the card, using the `products` array that `src/lib/products.ts` exports. The output is the HTML React made.
examples.output:
Trailhead

Trail Pack 45L

$189.00

Camp Kettle 1L

$34.00
examples.explanation: `products` is a `Product[]`, so `products[0]` is a product, the Trail Pack, and `products[2]` is the Camp Kettle. Until the course's later lessons fetch products from a server, they're written straight into that file. The first card leaves out `size`, so the default, `"md"`, made its class `card card-md`. The second passed `"sm"`. The markup was written once, and each card shows its own data. Change the card's file, and both cards change. `export default` makes `App` the file's main export, which is how the project from the next lesson expects to find it.

examples.title: A mistake TypeScript catches
examples.prompt: Two mistakes in `src/App.tsx`, checked with `npx tsc -b`, the type check the next lesson sets up. This is what it printed.
examples.output:
src/App.tsx:7:42 - error TS2322: Type '"large"' is not assignable to type '"md" | "sm" | undefined'.

7       <ProductCard product={products[0]} size="large" />
                                           ~~~~

  src/components/ProductCard.tsx:6:3 - The expected type comes from property 'size' which is declared here on type 'IntrinsicAttributes & ProductCardProps'
    6   size?: "sm" | "md";
        ~~~~

src/App.tsx:8:20 - error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'Product'.

8       <ProductCard product="Camp Kettle 1L" />
                     ~~~~~~~

  src/components/ProductCard.tsx:5:3 - The expected type comes from property 'product' which is declared here on type 'IntrinsicAttributes & ProductCardProps'
    5   product: Product;
        ~~~~~~~


Found 2 errors in the same file, starting at: src/App.tsx:7
examples.explanation: Each error names the file, the line, and the column, like `src/App.tsx:7:42`, then the problem, then the line itself with `~` under the mistake. Line 7 passes a size the union doesn't allow, and the message lists what it does allow: `"md"`, `"sm"`, or `undefined`, which is what an optional prop is when it's left out. The indented lines under each error point at where the rule comes from, in the card's props type. Line 8 passes a string where a whole product belongs. Without types, the first card would quietly get a class nobody styled, and the second would show an empty heading and crash on its price. Your editor underlines both lines the moment you type them, long before anyone opens the page.

steps.title: Children and composition

examples.title: One frame, two kinds of content
examples.prompt: `src/App.tsx` puts a product card in one `Card` and a login prompt in another. The output is the HTML React made.
examples.output:
Picked for you

Trail Pack 45L

$189.00

Members save 10%

Log in to see member prices.

Log in
examples.explanation: The first card's children is one element, the product card. The second card's children is two elements, a paragraph and a link, which React passes as an array. `Card` handles both the same way, since `{children}` shows whatever it's given. In the output, each `section` has its `h2` first and then exactly what was written between the tags. Notice that `Card` never imports `ProductCard`. The parent, `App`, decides what goes inside, so `Card` can frame things that didn't exist when it was written.

examples.title: A page layout with slots
examples.prompt: A layout every page can share, in `src/components/PageLayout.tsx`, with a slot for the header, a slot for a sidebar, and `children` for the page's own content.
examples.explanation: Each slot is typed `ReactNode`, so it takes any JSX at all, and the layout places it inside the right HTML element: `header`, `aside` for content beside the main part, `main`, and `footer`. Those are the meaningful elements from the web course's HTML lessons, so screen readers can jump between the page's regions. The footer's text is fixed, since it's the same on every page. A product page and a cart page would each render a `PageLayout` with their own header and sidebar, and the structure, the order, and the styling of the page live in this one file. To add a banner to every page, you'd change only this layout.

steps.title: Showing things only sometimes

examples.title: In stock, or sold out
examples.prompt: A card in `src/components/StockCard.tsx` that uses the conditional operator and `&&`, shown for the Trail Pack, which is in stock, and the Alpine tent, which isn't. The output is the HTML React made.
examples.output:
Trail Pack 45L

$189.00

Alpine 1P Tent

Sold out

Email me when it's back
examples.explanation: The paragraph is always there, and the conditional operator picks what goes in it: the price, or Sold out. The link is all or nothing. For the Trail Pack, `!product.inStock` is `false`, so the `&&` gives `false` and React shows nothing, with no empty tag or gap left behind. For the tent, it's `true`, so the `&&` gives the link. The parentheses around the link only let it spread over two lines, and the link's address is a template literal that puts the slug in. The same component, given different data, describes a different screen.

examples.title: A stray zero
examples.prompt: A cart link in `src/components/CartLink.tsx` that shows a badge with the number of items, rendered with `count={0}` and then `count={2}`. The output is the HTML React made.
examples.explanation: With two items, `2 && <span>` gives the span, and the badge shows 2. With an empty cart, `0 && <span>` gives `0`, and since React shows numbers, a 0 sits right after the word Cart, so the link reads Cart0. It's one of the most common React bugs, and it hides well, since it only shows up when something is empty. Change the condition to `count > 0 && ...`, which is `true` or `false`, and the empty cart shows nothing at all. Any time the left side of `&&` is a number, turn it into a comparison first.

steps.title: Lists and keys
steps.body:
Most screens show lists that come from data: products, reviews, the lines in a cart. You don't write each item by hand. You turn the data into elements, and you give each one a key, so that when the list changes, React can tell which item is which. Getting the key right is what keeps a list fast, and keeps what's typed in a row with the right row. ## From data to elements `map` makes a new array by calling a function on each item, the array method from the web course. Map an array of products to an array of elements, put the result in braces, and React shows each element in order: ```tsx
    {products.map((product) => (
  • {product.name}
    • ))}
``` The function passed to `map` is an arrow function, and the parentheses around the JSX let it span lines while it still returns the element. ## Keys Every element in a list needs a `key` prop: a string or number that's unique among its siblings and stays the same from one render to the next. The best key is an id that comes with the data, like a product's slug or an id the server gave it. React reads the key itself, so your component doesn't receive it as a prop. It's the `key` field you saw on the element object in the first part. Leave the key out, and React still shows the list, and warns you in the console, as the second example shows. The warning matters, because of what happens next. ## Why React matches by key When a list changes, React compares the new list with the old one to work out the fewest DOM changes, the diffing from the Why React Exists lesson. The key is how it pairs them up: an item with the same key is the same item, wherever it moved. ```diagram components-and-jsx-keys With real keys, sorting moves nodes. With index keys, every row gets the next product's text. ``` In the top half of the diagram, the products are keyed by slug. After sorting by price, React sees the same three keys in a new order, so it moves the three existing DOM nodes and changes nothing inside them. Anything in a row, like text someone typed into a note field, or which field has focus, goes with its product. The bottom half uses each item's position in the array, its index, as the key, which is what React falls back on when you give no key. After sorting, keys 0, 1, and 2 all still exist, so React thinks nothing moved and rewrites the text of every row instead. Worse, anything typed into the first row stays in the first row, now next to a different product. So: - **Use an id from the data.** Make one when you create the item, and store it with the item, never while rendering. - **Use the index only for a list that never changes order**, never filters, and never gets items in the middle. - **Never use a random key**, like `Math.random()`. A new key every render tells React every item is new, so it throws away and rebuilds the whole list each time. ## Filter and sort first To show some of the items, or in another order, change the array before you map it: ```tsx const shown = products .filter((product) => product.inStock) .toSorted((a, b) => a.priceCents - b.priceCents); ``` `filter` keeps the items its function says yes to. `toSorted` returns a sorted copy, and its function compares two items: a negative result puts `a` first. Use `toSorted`, not `sort`, because `sort` reorders the array in place, and that array is a prop, which a component must never change. ## Two elements per item Sometimes each item becomes two elements side by side, like a term and its description in a `dl`. A plain fragment can't take a key, so use the long form, `Fragment`, imported from React: ```tsx {specs.map((spec) => (
{spec.label}
{spec.value}
 ))} ```

examples.title: In stock, cheapest first
examples.prompt: `src/components/ProductList.tsx` lists the products that are in stock, cheapest first. It was given the shop's four products. The output is the HTML React made.
examples.explanation: Of the four products, two are in stock, so `filter` kept the Trail Pack and the Camp Kettle. `toSorted` put the cheaper one first, and `map` turned each into an `li` keyed by its slug. The `products` prop wasn't changed at all: `filter` and `toSorted` each made a new array, and `shown` is the last one. Doing this work during rendering is fine, since it's quick and always matches the current props. The keys don't show up in the HTML, because they're for React alone.

examples.title: The warning for a missing key
examples.prompt: The same list without keys, in `src/components/NoKeyList.tsx`. The page shows all four names, and this appeared in the browser's console, in red.
examples.output:
Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop.

Check the render method of `NoKeyList`. See https://react.dev/link/warning-keys for more information.
examples.explanation: React shows the list anyway, keyed by position, and tells you which component to fix. You'll only see this message while developing, since React leaves its warnings out of the build you put online, so keep the console open as you work. The project's linter, which the next lesson sets up, catches it even earlier: it flagged this line with Missing "key" prop for element in iterator, before the page ever ran. The fix is one attribute, `key={product.slug}` on the `li`.

steps.title: Styling components
steps.body:
A component bundles its markup and what it does, and its styles need a home too. Where they live decides whether you can change one component's look without breaking another's, and that matters more as an app grows to hundreds of components written by several people.

## Plain CSS files

The simplest way is an ordinary stylesheet, imported from JavaScript: `import "./ProductCard.css";` at the top of the component's file. Vite adds it to the page, as the web course showed. The catch is that every rule in it applies to the whole page. Two components that both style a class called `title` will fight, and the one whose CSS loads last wins. On a small site you can manage that by hand. On a large one, nobody can be sure what a change will break.

## Tailwind in className

This course styles Trailhead with Tailwind, the utility classes from the web course: each class does one small job, and Tailwind scans your files and makes CSS for only the classes you use. In React they go in `className`, and they fit components well, since a component's styles sit right in its markup, and removing a component removes its styles. The first example styles the product card this way.

## Classes that depend on props

Often a class depends on a prop: a smaller card, a faded one when sold out. You could build the string with template literals and ternaries, and it gets hard to read fast. **clsx** is a tiny package, a few hundred bytes, made for this. Install it with `npm install clsx`. It takes any number of arguments and joins the ones that are strings, skipping `false`, `null`, and `undefined`:

```tsx
clsx("rounded-lg border", size === "sm" && "p-3", !product.inStock && "opacity-60")
```

For a small sold-out card, that's `"rounded-lg border p-3 opacity-60"`. Each condition reads on its own, and a false one leaves no stray space or word behind.

One rule from the web course's Tailwind lesson matters even more in components: write every class name out in full. A name pieced together from parts at run time, like `p-` plus a size, never appears whole in your files, so Tailwind's scanner can't find it, and the class gets no CSS. Pick from whole names in an object instead, as the first example does with `sizes`.

## CSS Modules

If you'd rather write ordinary CSS, **CSS Modules** keep it from clashing. Name the file with `.module.css`, like `Badge.module.css`:

```css
.badge {
  padding: 2px 8px;
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: #e7e5e4;
}

.sale {
  background: #fde68a;
}
```

Import it as an object, `import styles from "./Badge.module.css";`, and use `styles.badge` as the class. Vite gives each class a new name made unique to that file, so a `.badge` in another module can never clash with this one. Vite supports CSS Modules with no setup, and the second example shows the names it makes.

## Inline styles for values you only know at run time

The `style` prop takes an object, not a string, with the CSS properties in camelCase: `style={{ backgroundColor: "white" }}`. The outer braces hold the expression, and the inner ones make the object. A plain number means pixels for sizes, so `{ width: 120 }` is 120px.

Keep inline styles for values you can't know until the code runs, like the width of a rating bar, which comes from the data. Inline styles can't use `:hover`, media queries, or dark mode, and they're hard to override, so everything else belongs in classes.

## Which to choose

Most teams pick one way for the whole app and stick to it. Tailwind with clsx is common on new projects and is what this course uses. CSS Modules are common too, especially on teams that like writing CSS. You'll meet both at work, and plain CSS files in older code.

None of this runs yet, since there's no project to run it in. The next lesson, Starting a New React Project, makes one on your computer, so you can try every example from this one.

examples.title: The product card with Tailwind and clsx
examples.prompt: The product card from earlier, styled with Tailwind classes, in `src/components/ProductCard.tsx`. It's shown for the Trail Pack at the default size, then for the sold-out tent at size sm. The output is the HTML React made.
examples.output:
Trail Pack 45L

$189.00

Alpine 1P Tent

$279.00
examples.explanation: The classes every card shares come first. `sizes[size]` picks the padding and text size by name from an object of whole class strings, so Tailwind's scanner sees all four classes. `!product.inStock && "opacity-60"` fades a sold-out card, and for an in-stock one it's `false`, which clsx skips. In the output, the Trail Pack got `p-5 text-base` and no fade, and the tent got `p-3 text-sm opacity-60`. When the TypeScript union for `size` gains a new value, TypeScript makes you add it to `sizes` too, since `sizes[size]` must exist for every allowed size.

examples.title: A badge with a CSS Module
examples.prompt: `src/components/Badge.tsx` uses the `Badge.module.css` file above, and was rendered as a plain badge and a sale badge. The output is the HTML React made while developing.
examples.explanation: `styles.badge` held `_badge_67nvu_1`: the class name from the stylesheet, a short code that stands for the file, and the line the rule starts on. The `.badge` rule in the stylesheet was renamed the same way, so the two still match, and a `.badge` in any other module gets a different code. clsx adds the sale class only when `tone` is `"sale"`. The names change when the file moves or the rule moves to another line, so never type a module's class name into code or tests by hand. Always go through `styles`.

examples.title: An inline style for a rating
examples.prompt: A bar that fills to a product's average rating, in `src/components/RatingBar.tsx`, rendered for an average of 4.2. The output is the HTML React made.
examples.explanation: The bar's color, size, and rounding are fixed, so they're Tailwind classes. Only the width depends on the data, so only the width is inline: 4.2 out of 5 is 84%. React turned the object into the `style` attribute you see in the output. A bar means nothing to someone using a screen reader, so `role="img"` and `aria-label`, from the web course's HTML lessons, tell it to read the bar as Rated 4.2 out of 5. The inner `div` closes itself with `/>`, since it has no children.

recap:
- JSX compiles to `jsx()` calls, and each call returns an element: a plain object describing what to show.
- Braces hold expressions, attributes use DOM names like `className` and `htmlFor`, every tag closes, and a fragment groups tags with no wrapper.
- A component is a capitalized function that takes one props object and returns JSX, and TypeScript types say what each prop holds.
- Props are read-only, and a component is pure: the same props give the same JSX, and it changes nothing outside itself.
- `children` and other props can hold JSX, so you build bigger components by composition, not inheritance.
- Show things sometimes with an early return, the conditional operator, `&&`, or `null`, and never put a bare number left of `&&`.
- Map data to elements with a stable key from the data, and filter and sort copies before you map them.
- Style with Tailwind and clsx or with CSS Modules, and keep inline styles for values known only at run time.
